summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with data objects for monitoring and managing the NTP entity on a host using SNMP. This lets operators watch time synchronization in a platform- and vendor-independent way. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A dashboard for a clock-keeping program. It lets managers look at how well the computer's time is being kept, using one common set of labels.

questions: how to monitor ntp with snmp
what notifications does the ntp mib define
subtitle: A standard set of SNMP-readable objects for monitoring and managing a host's NTP time service.

tldr.problem: Time synchronization is mission-critical, yet operators had no standard, vendor-independent way to monitor an NTP service.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5907 defines the NTPv4-MIB, an SNMP Management Information Base with objects for entity information, current status, each association, a few controls, and notifications for key events.
tldr.outcome: Operators can query NTP state and receive notifications such as mode changes, stratum changes and a periodic heartbeat. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5907 is a Proposed Standard from June 2010, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It manages NTP as defined in RFC 5905.

sections.title: Purpose of the NTPv4 MIB
sections.content:
The NTPv4 MIB module lets the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) monitor and manage local NTP entities, where NTP is the protocol from RFC 5905. It offers data objects that can be queried and that represent the current status of the NTP entity.

These cover general information about the entity (vendor, product, version) and connectivity to upstream NTP servers and hardware reference clocks such as radio clocks. The most important values are included so that failures can be detected before they affect overall time synchronization. The module also defines notifications for state changes, and objects to control those notifications.
sections.eli5: Many computers keep time by asking other clocks. This gives managers a standard way to peek at whether that clock-asking is going well.

sections.title: The Management Framework It Plugs Into
sections.content:
Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), usually accessed through SNMP. Objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is written in SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580 (all STD 58). For an overview of the framework the RFC points to Section 7 of RFC 3410.

The RFC does not describe SNMP itself. It only supplies a new module of named objects that fit the existing framework.
sections.eli5: SNMP is the way managers ask devices questions. A MIB is the list of questions you are allowed to ask, and this RFC writes the list for clocks.

sections.title: How the Module Is Organized
sections.content:
The module is divided into sections: general server information, current NTP entity status, status of all mobilized associations (unicast upstream time servers, multicast or broadcast, time references and hardware clocks), NTP entity control objects, objects used only in notifications, and the SNMP notification definitions for core events.

The general information section is static and identifies which NTP implementation runs on the host: vendor and product name, version, hardware and OS platform, and the time resolution of the OS. The control section currently contains two objects, one for the heartbeat interval and one to enable or disable each notification. The notification-only section has one object, a cleartext event message.

Some values appear both as numbers and as human-readable strings. If the two differ, the numeric one takes precedence. The module is registered as ntpSnmpMIB under { mib-2 197 }.
sections.eli5: The dashboard has pages: who made the clock program, how the clock is doing now, which other clocks it listens to, a few switches, and alarm bells.

sections.title: Entity Information and Status Objects
sections.content:
The information group holds read-only strings and numbers such as the software name (for example ntpd), version, vendor, system type, time resolution, precision and the distance to the root time reference at stratum 0.

The status group reports the current state. ntpEntStatusCurrentMode is one of notRunning, notSynchronized, noneConfigured, syncToLocal, syncToRefclock, syncToRemoteServer or unknown. Other objects give the entity's stratum, the ID and name of the current system peer, the offset to it, the number of configured sources, root dispersion, entity uptime, the NTP date and time, the next known leap second and its direction, and packet counters (in, out, bad version, protocol errors, notifications). A table counts packets sent and received per packet mode, such as client, server and broadcast.

The NtpStratum textual convention allows 1 to 16, with 16 meaning no stratum. The date and time object is in the 128-bit NTP date format and is zero-length when unsynchronized. It is meant for timestamping events, not for setting a node's clock, and the RFC says NTP, or at least SNTP, should be used for that.
sections.eli5: The status page says whether the clock is running, whether it trusts another clock, how far off it is and how many messages it has handled.

sections.title: Associations and Their Statistics
sections.content:
An association is a time reference the entity is working with. The association table is indexed by an internal unique ID (ntpAssocId, 1 to 99999). Each row holds a name, the refclock driver ID where one applies, the address type and address (IPv4 or IPv6, with or without zone index), the offset, stratum, jitter, delay and root dispersion.

A second table, indexed the same way, keeps per-association counters of packets in, packets out and protocol errors. As with the entity counters, discontinuities can occur on cold start or reinitialization of the NTP entity.
sections.eli5: Each clock your computer listens to gets its own row, with how far off it is, how long messages take, and how many messages came and went.

sections.title: Control Objects and Notifications
sections.content:
Two objects are writable. ntpEntHeartbeatInterval sets, in seconds, how often the heartbeat notification is sent; its default is 60, and if it is 0 with the heartbeat bit enabled the notification is sent once. ntpEntNotifBits has one bit per notification, where 1 enables it and 0 disables it. Both values are stored persistently and restored after a cold start or restart.

Eight notifications are defined for core events: mode change, stratum change, system peer changed, association added, association removed, configuration changed, leap second announced, and a heartbeat that shows the entity is still alive. Most carry the NTP date and time plus the cleartext message object. The heartbeat also carries the current mode and the heartbeat interval. The RFC describes the heartbeat and a test notification as tools for checking that notifications are received and that the entity is up.
sections.eli5: There are two switches: how often to say 'I am still alive', and which alarm bells are turned on. The alarms ring when something important changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two objects are read-write, and unprotected SET operations can hurt network operations. Setting ntpEntHeartbeatInterval to 1 makes the entity send one notification each second, which is the maximum automatic rate, and repeated writes can produce notifications faster. ntpEntNotifBits could be used to switch off notifications and delay or hide critical events.

Readable objects can be sensitive too. The software name, version, vendor and system type could help an attacker find known problems. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security, so the RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and leaves it to the operator to grant access only to legitimate principals.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can flip the switches could silence the alarms or flood you with messages, and the label on the clock program could tell a burglar which lock to pick. So only let trusted people in, using secure SNMP.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The module uses one IANA-assigned object identifier value, recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: ntpSnmp is { mib-2 197 }. No other registrations are described.
sections.eli5: The module gets one official number in the big phone book of managed things, so it never clashes with anyone else's.

items.label: notSynchronized
items.desc: Not synchronized to any time source (stratum 16).

items.label: noneConfigured
items.desc: Not synchronized and no reference configured (stratum 16).

items.label: syncToLocal
items.desc: Distributing time from its local clock, with degraded accuracy or reliability.

items.label: syncToRefclock
items.desc: Synchronized to a local hardware reference clock such as GPS.

items.label: syncToRemoteServer
items.desc: Synchronized to a remote upstream NTP server.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The state of NTP is unknown.

items.label: ntpEntNotifModeChange
items.desc: The NTP entity changes mode, including starting and stopping.

items.label: ntpEntNotifSyspeerChanged
items.desc: A new system peer has been selected.

items.label: ntpEntNotifLeapSecondAnnounced
items.desc: A leap second has been announced.

items.label: ntpEntNotifHeartbeat
items.desc: Sent periodically to show the entity is still alive.
